a_rows_sample.anchor: There may be an **infinite number of propositions believed, while only a finite number are ever represented**; reasoning bridges the gap between what is represented and what is believed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Treated as a major direct support for the infinite Knowledge Space hypothesis: R_t^A ⊂ K_t^A ⊂ Ω where Ω=unbounded Knowledge Space, K_t^A=what participant A believes/knows at time t, R_t^A=what is explicitly represented, with |R_t^A|<|K_t^A|<|Ω| as conceptual (not literal measurable) cardinality comparisons; reasoning bridges the gap between what is represented and what is believed, adding a REPRESENTATION and REASONING layer between the infinite space and the epistemic state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: representation \neq knowledge ... language \neq semantic object
a_rows_sample.statement: The book defines representation as a relationship where one domain 'stands for' another (e.g. the symbolic sentence 'John loves Mary' represents the abstract proposition John loves Mary); the symbol is concrete/manipulable, the proposition abstract — validating representation != knowledge and language != semantic object as one of the strongest cross-book invariants found. Architecture retains three layers: Expression (words/sentences/diagrams/code/documents), Semantic (propositions/concepts/relations), Epistemic (beliefs/commitments/knowledge attribution).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knows(a,p,t,c)
a_rows_sample.statement: 'John knows that p' is a relation between a knower and an abstract proposition that can be true or false, surviving all lenses as Knows(a,p,t,c) (participant, proposition, time, context) — surprisingly close to the Williamson direction. But Brachman & Levesque add an operational separation Williamson did not give: KB(a) (operational representation) is not equivalent to Knows(a,p) (philosophical knowledge relation); the KB is a representation supporting reasoning about what the agent knows/believes — this is exactly where the KnowledgeOS Kernel should operate.

a_rows_sample.anchor: an intelligent process can contain structural elements which observers interpret as representing a propositional account of the process's knowledge, and which also play a causal role in generating the system's behavior.
a_rows_sample.statement: The book's 'Knowledge Representation Hypothesis' (attributed to Brian Smith): a representation is not useful merely because it describes a system but because it can causally participate in behavior. Gives an engineering test: a stored representation is more than passive information when its semantic content is explicitly represented AND the reasoning/decision process is designed to operate on that content — illustrated by two near-identical Prolog programs where only the one with an explicit KB (vs hard-coded procedures) counts as knowledge-based.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ### Knowledge level ... ### Symbol level
a_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge level (what is represented, what it means, what follows, expressiveness, entailment) vs Symbol level (data structures, algorithms, computational architecture, algorithmic complexity) maps almost exactly to KnowledgeOS Semantic/Epistemic Space -> Kernel contract -> implementation (database/graph/vector index/LLM/solver) — 'an excellent architectural boundary.' The book explicitly treats FOL as only a starting point, not committed to any particular language or to reasoning as entailment computation, confirming that the KnowledgeOS Kernel should not be 'the universal logic of knowledge.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: ## Explicitness Principle
a_rows_sample.statement: The book distinguishes explicit beliefs (in the KB) from implicit beliefs (entailments only implicitly given), promoted to a KnowledgeOS Explicitness Principle: E_t ⊆ I_t where E_t=explicitly represented knowledge/commitments, I_t=what is implicitly available under the reasoning regime (e.g. 'Election E is legally valid' need not be stored if 'all certified elections are legally valid' and 'Election E is certified' are explicit). Suggests candidate metrics ExpansionRatio=|Implicit(KB)|/|Explicit(KB)| and DerivationDepth(p) (inference steps needed to derive p), giving mathematical meaning to 'knowledge can become deeper by connecting concepts.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: First-order entailment is in general undecidable... Expressiveness ↔ Tractability
a_rows_sample.statement: First-order entailment is in general undecidable; the book frames Expressiveness <-> Tractability as a fundamental tradeoff (more expressive representations make reasoning substantially harder). For the infinite Knowledge Space idea this means: the semantic space may be unbounded while every operational projection must be bounded by computational capacity — proposes Capacity=(RepresentationalCapacity E(L), ReasoningCapacity R(L,A,T)) and Knowledge Projection=f(representation capacity, reasoning capacity, available information), and a boundary B=B_semantic ∩ B_context ∩ B_resource, noting 'representable ≠ tractably reasoned.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: nonlogical symbols do not have one universal meaning; their interpretation is application-dependent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Symbol meaning is application-dependent (e.g. 'approval' differs across software deployment/election governance/financial authorization/legal proceedings), validating that Meaning(word) is not constant but Meaning(symbol | context, interpretation) — strongly supporting the existing Context/Boundary/Level-of-Abstraction architecture and the Projection idea (same symbolic structure interpreted differently, e.g. 'john' referring to different individuals depending on interpretation).

a_rows_sample.anchor: defeasible inheritance, default reasoning, nonmonotonicity, closed-world assumptions, multiple default extensions
a_rows_sample.statement: The book's coverage of defeasible inheritance/default reasoning/nonmonotonicity confirms knowledge cannot always be modelled as monotonic accumulation of facts (a projection can add/withdraw/override/except/revise), aligning with Gärdenfors and Gelfond/Kahl. Its uncertainty chapter separates vagueness, uncertainty, objective probability, subjective probability, Bayesian belief, and Dempster-Shafer theory, supporting 'there is no reason to force uncertainty, vagueness and probability into a single metric', reinforcing the Knowledge Measurement Vector over a knowledge_score. Also notes a 'Vivid Knowledge' chapter treating analogues/diagrams/models as legitimate representational projections beyond language/text.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 1. There is an underlying world/domain. 2. A participant has beliefs/knowledge about it. 3. Only part of that knowledge may be explicitly represented...
a_rows_sample.statement: Zero-Lens extraction on Brachman & Levesque (removing FOL/Prolog/frames/description logic/SAT/default logic/Bayesian networks/STRIPS/GOLOG) yields twelve survivor claims: an underlying world/domain exists; a participant has beliefs/knowledge about it; only part is explicitly represented; representation is a mapping between domains; reasoning derives implicit content from explicit content; meaning depends on interpretation/context; different representation languages have different expressive power; reasoning capability is resource-limited; knowledge changes and can be revised; uncertainty/vagueness require richer representations; the same knowledge may have different representations; action depends on knowledge — described as extraordinarily close to the current model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson → what knowledge may fundamentally be. Brachman/Levesque → how knowledge can be operationally represented/reasoned about.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit division of labor: Williamson tells us what knowledge may fundamentally be (factive relation); Brachman/Levesque tell us how knowledge can be operationally represented/reasoned about — the book does not itself establish the factive-relation claim. Final refined definitions: Knowledge is a factive epistemic relation between a participant and content about some domain, while a knowledge representation is a finite, context-dependent symbolic/structural projection of what the participant can make explicit and reason with, and may be incomplete relative to both the participant's broader knowledge and the unbounded Knowledge Space; Knowledge Space is the unbounded domain of possible facts/propositions/entities/relations/states/interpretations/institutional structures/inferential connections; KnowledgeOS preserves/manages finite time-dependent representations and epistemic histories while allowing multiple reasoning regimes to construct projections/derive implicit content/evaluate uncertainty/explain/compare views.

a_rows_sample.anchor: It does **not** establish: Knowledge Space is literally infinite ... Knowledge can be assigned one scalar quantity ... KnowledgeOS should implement FOL ... KnowledgeOS should implement an ontology
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit honesty about limits: the book does NOT establish that Knowledge Space is literally infinite, that knowledge is literally movement through a universal space, that knowledge has one universal mathematical representation, that knowledge can be assigned one scalar quantity, or that KnowledgeOS should implement FOL or an ontology — these remain architectural hypotheses informed by multiple lenses. The strongest direct support is only for: finite representation vs broader knowledge, multiple representation regimes, implicit vs explicit content, context-dependent meaning, reasoning over representations, computational limits.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Representation Capacity ≠ Knowledge Capacity ≠ Reasoning Capacity
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Representation capacity RC(L) (how much semantic structure can be encoded), Reasoning capacity RCog(L,A,T) (how much can be derived under algorithm A within resource bound T), and Knowledge projection capacity KC(S,A,R,T) (how much of a target scope the system can make operationally available) as three different quantities. Gives a final Kernel diagram (Identity/Content/Context/Participant/Proposition/Boundary/Time/Representation/Provenance/Interpretation/Commitment/Input/Assessment/History/Transition preserved, feeding declared Logic/Probabilistic/Nonmonotonic regimes) and three named principles: Representation-Reasoning Separation, Finite Representation/Unbounded Knowledge Principle, and Expressiveness-Tractability Principle.

b_rows_sample.anchor: TRUE != BELIEVED != KNOWN / ASSERTED != ACCEPTED != TRUE / CONFIDENCE != TRUTH / UNKNOWN != FALSE ... Absence of knowledge must not be represented as falsehood.
b_rows_sample.statement: Williamson's contribution: knowledge is not whatever an agent believes, has epistemic requirements and intrinsic limits; motivates an explicit state vocabulary (UNKNOWN, ABSENT, INSUFFICIENT, QUESTIONABLE, CONFLICTED, REJECTED, VALIDATED, SUPERSEDED, WITHDRAWN) with the exact governed vocabulary left as a domain-law question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS must never silently turn "supported" or "probable" into "known."
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is factive: a factive attitude can only be directed toward truths; Williamson treats knowing as the most general factive stative attitude, distinct from believed(P)/supported(P)/probable(P)/asserted(P), all of which 'may be false' while known(P) is factive. This should be a Kernel-level safeguard: never silently convert 'supported' or 'probable' into 'known'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson rejects the assumption that knowledge can be completely separated into an internal mental part and an external-world part... he explicitly describes knowledge as broad
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is broad: K_A(P) depends not only on A's internal representation but on the external world, context, object of knowledge, and relevant environment. This revises the earlier Agent->projection->Knowledge Space model: the agent does not invent the space, the agent's knowledge is constitutively connected to the space (KNOWLEDGE SPACE Ω -> external world/social reality/semantic structures -> participant/agent -> capacity+access -> epistemic state).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Capacity is not knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: A Williamson-inspired correction to the earlier 'knowledge might be a capacity to write information and define its scope' idea: capacity is not knowledge. A system can have high representation capacity (an LLM generating text, a database storing petabytes) without knowing anything. Instead: capacity determines what a participant can potentially represent/investigate/distinguish/communicate; knowledge is a factive epistemic relation/state involving the participant and the external target (CAPACITY -> access/observation/reasoning -> epistemic state -> KNOWLEDGE).

b_rows_sample.anchor: He argues for the **primeness** of knowledge and warns against decomposing it into composite conditions when doing so loses explanatory generality.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge may be prime (non-composite): a maximally detailed decomposition can make an explanation worse by destroying useful generalization. This strengthens the earlier Merricks 'non-redundant work' principle (a candidate primitive deserves first-class status if removing it destroys non-redundant capability) into two tests: the Reduction test ('Can X be reconstructed?') and the Primeness test ('Does treating X as a composite destroy explanatory/general structure?').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson argues that people are not always in a position to know whether they know something. He calls the mistaken assumption that important mental conditions are cognitively transparent **luminosity** and argues against it.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is not luminous (anti-luminosity): KnowledgeOS cannot assume a participant can perfectly report the state of its own knowledge. 'Agent says I know P' is itself an assertion requiring evaluation; 'Agent says I don't know P' does not necessarily prove P is outside its epistemic capacity. This is a major correction to the previous model of UNKNOWN, requiring KnowledgeOS to distinguish KNOWLEDGE / KNOWLEDGE ABOUT KNOWLEDGE (K_A(K_A(P))) / SELF-ASSESSMENT / EXTERNAL ASSESSMENT / COMPUTATIONAL ESTIMATE as non-equivalent layers, with the second not automatically following from the first.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The agent's **self-report of knowledge** is therefore an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.
b_rows_sample.statement: For an AI agent claiming 'I know that the architecture decision is valid', KnowledgeOS should be able to represent P, the AI's claim knows(P), the supporting evidence, an external assessment (e.g. 'insufficient'), and the actual status ('unresolved') separately — the agent's self-report of knowledge is an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson's Chapter 5 investigates margins and "close possibilities."
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge has a margin: an agent may know P under ordinary circumstances but not under arbitrary tiny variations, so knowledge is not simply a point (TRUE) but can have a 'neighbourhood of epistemic safety'. Proposed quantity M(P,A,C) represents the size/structure of the range of relevant variations under which the knowledge attribution remains stable (not a final formula) — high margin means knowledge remains stable under nearby changes, low margin means small changes may destroy knowledge. This connects the topological lens to epistemology: 'What kinds of changes would invalidate the knowledge attribution?'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson discusses contextual variation in epistemic standards but does not reduce truth/knowledge to arbitrary subjective standards.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is contextual but not arbitrarily relative: different epistemic contexts (S_t^A, S_t^B, S_t^G) can differ in their knowledge attributions, but this does not mean 'everything is equally true' — different knowledge attributions still point to the same underlying Knowledge Space, supporting the idea that different participants are oriented toward the same infinite space.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson separates causal basis from evidential basis.
b_rows_sample.statement: Cause of belief is not the same as evidence for belief: a perceptual process can be probabilistically caused by the environment without the resulting evidence itself being probabilistic in the same way. This is a non-collapse rule — KnowledgeOS must preserve both relationships (causal basis, evidential basis) separately.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson's Chapters 9–10 develop the idea that **knowledge itself can function as evidence**, and he explicitly identifies one's evidence with what one knows within his framework.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge can be evidence (E=K): observation -> knowledge -> evidence for another proposition -> new knowledge, a recursive structure where the Knowledge Space is not simply 'evidence -> knowledge' but can contain 'knowledge -> evidence -> inference -> knowledge', making knowledge a participating element in reasoning, not merely a final storage state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: He explicitly shows that evidential probability 1 should not be treated as absolute certainty, and that treating evidence as permanently probability-1 creates an implausible monotonicity problem. New evidence can undermine something previously regarded as evidence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Evidential probability 1 must not be treated as absolute certainty; treating evidence as permanently probability-1 creates an implausible monotonicity problem since new evidence can undermine something previously regarded as evidence. This validates Gärdenfors's distinction between historical evidence and permanently-unquestionable evidence: KnowledgeOS evidence history should be immutable, but epistemic status may be revised.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Williamson's Chapter 11 argues for a **knowledge account of assertion**: the connection between knowing and asserting is not accidental.
b_rows_sample.statement: Assertion is downstream from knowledge (knowledge account of assertion): the earlier model 'knowledge -> language' is refined to KNOWLEDGE -> warrant to assert -> ASSERTION -> language/communication. The sentence itself is not the knowledge; the assertion act is a consequence of an epistemic state and a communicative norm, close to Searle's distinction between descriptive and constitutive/performative language.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ### K-INV-01 — Factivity cannot be silently violated
b_rows_sample.statement: Seven proposed Kernel invariants: K-INV-01 Factivity cannot be silently violated (a record labelled 'knowledge' cannot silently mean merely belief/claim); K-INV-02 Representation is not knowledge (storage alone confers no epistemic status); K-INV-03 Knowledge attribution is contextual (must identify participant, scope/context, time); K-INV-04 Self-report is not self-proof ('I know P' is not sufficient proof P is known); K-INV-05 Evidence can be revisable (historical evidence records remain, interpretation can change); K-INV-06 Knowledge history is reconstructible (a current projection must be traceable to its inputs/transformations); K-INV-07 No assumption of epistemic transparency (the system must permit 'I don't know that I don't know P' and incomplete metaknowledge generally).

b_rows_sample.anchor: ### Kernel should preserve
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposed Kernel boundary (inside/outside/above): Inside Kernel — identity, participant, context, boundary, time, representation provenance, observation/source, proposition/content reference, knowledge attribution, epistemic transition, evidence/history, relationships, conflict, revision/supersession, question/inquiry, assessment history, regime reference. Outside Kernel — words, sentences, documents, embeddings, LLMs, vector databases, specific statistical models, possible-world machinery, Bayesian machinery, Pramāṇa implementation, Pāṇinian grammar, topic taxonomy, UI, search algorithm, explanation algorithm. Above the Kernel — knowledge projections, topics, answers, explanations, reports, architecture views, governance views, AI-agent views. Knowledge is present in the Kernel not as Truth+Belief+Evidence but as a KNOWLEDGE ATTRIBUTION (participant -> knows -> proposition -> context/time/boundary/regime), respecting primeness while remaining operational.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel should not silently overwrite this into: P = KNOWLEDGE
b_rows_sample.statement: The Kernel should NOT decide whether P is 'knowledge' universally. Example: for P='System X is secure', KnowledgeOS may preserve 'Alice claims to know P', 'Audit A provides evidence E', 'Regime R assesses P', 'Verification V says unresolved', 'Bob says not proven' as a KnowledgeAttribution(participant, proposition, context, time, regime, provenance) without collapsing to P=KNOWLEDGE, allowing different epistemologies/regimes to coexist and evaluate independently.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Stop trying to construct "knowledge" bottom-up from representations.
b_rows_sample.statement: The biggest insight: stop trying to construct knowledge bottom-up from representations (words->sentences->propositions->evidence->truth->knowledge is conceptually backwards). Instead: Infinite Knowledge Space -> Knowledge relation/state, which can be represented, asserted, justified, serve as evidence, influence action, or be revised/lost. Representation is a downstream expression of a knowledge-bearing state, not what creates knowledge. This also re-interprets the earlier S_t=P(Ω|A,B,L,U,R,t,H) formula: it is not 'the state of Knowledge itself' but 'a projected epistemic representation of knowledge at t', and K_t^A(P) becomes a knowledge attribution 'Agent A knows P at time t under the relevant context/regime.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should not seek: KnowledgeScore ∈ [0,1] as the first objective. Instead quantify **properties of knowledge**
b_rows_sample.statement: Reject a universal KnowledgeScore ∈ [0,1]; instead quantify properties of knowledge Q(K,P,C,t) = (Evidence, Reliability, Margin, Coverage, Consistency, Relevance, Provenance, Stability). Candidate measurable properties: knowledge margin (how much nearby change before attribution fails), evidence contribution (removing evidence e, how much epistemic support changes — Williamson compares total-evidence hypothesis support against support after removing one item), explanatory value (how much knowing P improves prediction/explanation via probability/correlation), knowledge stability (how often an attribution is revised/lost under new evidence), projection coverage (how much declared scope has actually been represented).

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS must be able to represent uncertainty about its own epistemic boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Do not try to make the Kernel completely transparent to itself (anti-luminosity applied to the system itself); a system claiming to know exactly what it knows and does not know makes an extremely strong assumption. KnowledgeOS must represent uncertainty about its own epistemic boundary via states: KNOWN, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN WHETHER KNOWN, DISPUTED, OUTSIDE CURRENT MODEL, UNASSESSED — with 'unknown whether known' being particularly important.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Knowledge Space is an unbounded space of reality, meaning, institutional structures, events, relations and propositions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Final synthesis: 'The Knowledge Space is an unbounded space of reality, meaning, institutional structures, events, relations and propositions. Persons, machines and organizations have limited capacities and therefore form bounded, contextual, time-dependent projections of that space. Knowledge is a factive relation/state within such a projection—not merely information, representation, belief, evidence or truth alone. KnowledgeOS preserves the identities, contexts, provenance, temporal histories, epistemic transitions and knowledge attributions necessary for those projections to be reconstructed and evaluated under different regimes.' Capstone principle: KnowledgeOS must not confuse the projection with the space, the representation with the knowledge, or the epistemic assessment with reality — supported by McGinn, Floridi, Dretske, Fagin, Gärdenfors, Searle, and Williamson jointly.

b_notations: Timothy Williamson, Knowledge and Its Limits
a_aliases: Brachman & Levesque Knowledge Representation and Reasoning lens

a_rows_sample.anchor: Per 1600 section 5: construct Input -> Algorithm -> Output for every object; never accept "computable" as a statement. Five-class separation enforced.
a_rows_sample.statement: Standing rule (per an earlier document referenced as '1600 section 5'): for every object claimed computable, an explicit Input -> Algorithm -> Output construction must be produced; a bare assertion of computability is never accepted. Enforces a five-class computability separation: mathematically defined, algorithmically computable, practically computable, computable-only-with-human-judgement, and not identifiable from available observations.

Nothing is executed under this plan document itself.
a_rows_sample.statement: Restricts execution scope: any executable witnesses produced from this plan belong under a verification/ scratch directory only, never inside repository code paths, mirroring the discipline already applied to the GN-46 witnesses; and explicitly declares that this plan document itself executes nothing -- execution requires a later, separately authorized wave.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Prohibited conflations restated: MATHEMATICALLY DEFINED != OPERATIONALLY COMPUTABLE (eta is the standing example) - complexity claims require declared problem size and model (T-K10 discipline).
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates a prohibited conflation carried over from prior work: being mathematically defined is not the same as being operationally computable, with eta given as the standing example of the distinction; and restates that any complexity claim requires a declared problem size and computational model, per the 'T-K10' discipline.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Distinguish: 1. mathematically defined 2. theoretically computable 3. computationally tractable 4. practically computable 5. implemented 6. experimentally executed ... Defined != Computable. Computable != Implemented. Implemented != Executed. Executed != Mathematically Validated.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires distinguishing six non-equivalent levels for any mathematical object: mathematically defined, theoretically computable, computationally tractable, practically computable, implemented, and experimentally executed, summarized by four explicit non-equivalences: Defined != Computable, Computable != Implemented, Implemented != Executed, Executed != Mathematically Validated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero != Lord != Sarathi != Transition ... K_t -Zero-> Z_t -Lord-> L_t -Sarathi-> a_t -Commit-> e_t -delta-> K_{t+1} ... Zero, Lord, and Sarathi do not change K
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the initial Zero/Lord/Sarathi/Commit/Transition pipeline as a linear sequence culminating in a state change, with explicit invariants that Zero, Lord and Sarathi are each analytical (never transformational) and none of their outputs alone entail K_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sarathi should not 'recommend Commit'... Commitment is not an epistemic action. It is an authorization/governance action... a_t -Authorize-> c_t -Execute-> e_t. Guidance != Authorization != Execution != Transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Removes 'Commit' from Sarathi's action vocabulary and inserts an explicit Authorization boundary between recommendation and execution: Sarathi produces a recommendation a_t, Authorize(Knower,a_t,Policy) produces a command c_t, Execute(c_t) produces an event e_t, and only then does delta(K_t,e_t) fire -- Guidance != Authorization != Execution != Transition, with the missing Authorize function explicitly making the Knower's authority mathematically visible.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Execute: C -> E is too deterministic. Execution can fail... Execute(c_t) -> ExecutionResult in {Success(e),Failure(f),Partial(e,f)} ... ExecutionResult != DomainEvent.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Execute from a total deterministic function C->E to one returning a structured ExecutionResult (Success/Failure/Partial), and similarly Authorize to return an AuthorizationResult (Authorized/Rejected/Deferred/Modified) rather than assuming every recommendation becomes a command; ExecutionResult is explicitly distinguished from the DomainEvent that actually triggers a transition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the epistemic cycle is actually not always a cycle... External observation -> Event -> Transition can update the state directly... Guidance is optional; Transition is fundamental. G5 - Guidance is not a prerequisite for transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the closing theorem G5: Guidance (Zero/Lord/Sarathi) is not a prerequisite for every Knowledge-State transition -- a raw external observation event or a scheduled validity check can trigger delta(K_t,e_t) directly, so the lenses must never be modelled as mandatory middleware sitting between every event and the transition function; renames the pipeline from 'Epistemic Cycle' to 'Epistemic Guidance-and-Transition Cycle' to reflect this.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I strongly recommend introducing: I-hat_t = Candidate Ideal State and I_t = Approved Ideal State ... KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1} (proposal); Authorize(I-hat_{t+1}) -> I_{t+1}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a Candidate Ideal State (I-hat) vs Approved Ideal State (I) split mirroring the Q17 recommendation/authorization boundary: KnowledgeOS may only ever produce a candidate revision proposal, and only an explicit Authorize step (by the Knower/governance authority under applicable norms) produces the actually approved I_{t+1}; KnowledgeOS != I_{t+1} but KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi \rightarrow DecisionPosture
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sarathi's output from a binary Stop/Continue decision to a richer DecisionPosture ∈ {Proceed, Investigate, ProceedWithCaveats, Defer, Escalate, UnableToDecide}, argued to be closer to Sarathi's actual role.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Recommendation \neq Assertion
b_rows_sample.statement: Strict boundary: Recommendation ≠ Assertion, Recommendation ≠ Fact, Recommendation ≠ Decision. Sārathi may say 'Investigate the moral obligation dimension' but KnowledgeOS must not silently convert that into 'Therefore Arjuna should fight' — the Knower remains the decision authority unless the domain explicitly delegates that authority. Marked as extremely important for the DDD model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Lord needs a stronger boundary too: Candidate ≠ Knowledge, Candidate ≠ Evidence, Candidate ≠ Assertion. A presentation should visually distinguish KNOWN / INFERRED / UNKNOWN / CANDIDATE / RECOMMENDED to prevent semantic contamination.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(S_t) \rightarrow EpistemicFindings
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Zero's role as boundary-finder, not belief-decider: Zero(S_t) -> EpistemicFindings, Presentation ⊇ DecisionRelevant(EpistemicFindings); 'Zero does not decide what the Knower should believe. Zero says: Here is where the state has a boundary.' Also strengthens provenance: EveryDecisionRelevantClaim -> Provenance, with a worked claim-level provenance record example (Acquisition/Evidence/Observed-at/Validity/Conflict/Source).

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Unknown 
eq Absent 
eq NotApplicable 
eq NotObserved 
eq NotYetInvestigated
b_rows_sample.statement: Elevates 'unknown' to a fundamental principle already implicit in Zero: Unknown ≠ Absent ≠ NotApplicable ≠ NotObserved ≠ NotYetInvestigated, illustrated by Version=UNKNOWN not meaning Version=ABSENT, and SecurityStatus=NOT_ASSESSED not meaning SecurityStatus=SAFE.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero \neq UniversalValidator
b_rows_sample.statement: DDD warning that Zero risks becoming a 'god object' by owning detection of gaps, conflicts, type problems, temporal problems and epistemic boundaries all at once: Zero ≠ UniversalValidator. Zero is redefined narrowly as detecting epistemic boundaries/deficiencies relevant to current state and purpose, aggregating epistemic consequences of findings from separate domain validators (schema, type, policy, security violations).

b_rows_sample.anchor: LordCandidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: LordCandidate ≠ Knowledge and LordCandidate ≠ Evidence: Lord can propose 'there may be a moral-obligation dimension' but it becomes knowledge only after investigation; critical to prevent AI-generated hypotheses entering the Knowledge State as facts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: S\bar{a}rathiRecommendation \neq Decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Sārathi needs a constitutional policy boundary: SārathiRecommendation ≠ Decision, SārathiAction ≠ HumanAuthorization — Sārathi may determine the next best investigation, but the Knower decides whether to accept it unless the system has explicitly delegated authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (K,U,N,\Delta,P,Role) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action as too simplistic: Sārathi:(K,U,N,Δ,P,Role) -> Guidance, which may then produce Decision, which may then authorize Action, giving Guidance ≠ Decision ≠ Action (confirming an earlier DDD warning). Also reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as three functions/lenses over the state rather than three sequential stages: Zero=Diagnose, Lord=Reason/Synthesize/Orient, Sārathi=Guide, with Decision->Action occurring outside those lenses; explicitly an architectural abstraction, not a literal theological equivalence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (State, Norms, Role, Context, Discrepancies) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action (too direct) to Sārathi:(State,Norms,Role,Context,Discrepancies)->Guidance -> CandidateActions -> Decision -> Action, giving proper separation of concerns. Reaffirms Zero as a pure DiagnosticFunction that must not itself decide ('therefore do X'). Corrects Lord from 'merely a reasoning engine/LLM reasoning' to AuthoritativeKnowledge+NormativeOrientation+InterpretiveResolution, since Krishna in the text functions as an authoritative source of teaching, not just an inference engine — called crucial for KnowledgeOS governance. Confirms Sārathi = ContextualGuidance, distinguishing Lord ('what is authoritative/true/normative') from Sārathi ('how does that apply here') from Decision ('what will I choose') from Action ('what will I actually do').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(K,I,C,P) \rightarrow \text{Epistemic Boundaries}
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as product capabilities rather than domain entities: Zero(K,I,C,P)->Epistemic Boundaries acts as an 'epistemic diagnostic engine' (missing dimensions, unknown values, missing/weak/conflicting evidence, logical contradictions, stale knowledge, contextual mismatches, unresolved questions, unsupported assumptions, Ideal-State discrepancies); Lord asks 'what else might matter?' enabling 'horizon expansion' beyond gap-checking; Sārathi:(K,I,Z,L,Q,C)->NextAction performs 'epistemic navigation', worked through a Bhīṣma-relationship example (Zero flags unknown relationship, Lord flags kinship as material, Sārathi recommends investigating it before evaluating the decision).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can we migrate this Nexus installation?
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: asked 'Can we migrate this Nexus installation?', a conventional AI answers directly, while KnowledgeOS first constructs required dimensions (version, repository inventory, blob stores, storage, network, DNS, firewall, certificates, backup, dependencies, authentication, operational constraints), runs Zero to find missing items (backup verification, firewall confirmation, certificate ownership, dependency inventory), and has Sārathi respond 'Do not decide migration readiness yet. Investigate these four items.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: perform justified action given epistemic state
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts a conventional agent optimizing 'complete task' against KnowledgeOS optimizing 'perform justified action given epistemic state', worked through a deploy-approval example: required knowledge checklist (code reviewed✓, tests passed✓, architecture approved✓, security assessment✗, production configuration✗, rollback strategy✗) yields Zero='3 critical gaps' and Sārathi='DO NOT DEPLOY. Investigate security, configuration and rollback.' Also frames the agent loop as Understand Intent->Construct Knowledge State->Discover Dimensions->Zero->Identify Gaps/Conflicts->Lord->Expand Possible Investigation->Sārathi->Select Next Epistemic Action->Agent/Tool->Observation->Update Knowledge State->Repeat, called 'an epistemically governed autonomous agent architecture'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C) \rightarrow EvidenceCandidates
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects plain Retrieve(Query)->Documents to a goal-directed Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C)->EvidenceCandidates: the retrieval system 'knows why it is retrieving', discovering relevant dimensions (e.g. version, repository topology, blob stores, firewall, certificates for a migration decision) before retrieving. Zero can drive retrieval: given a partially-filled knowledge-state checklist, Zero reports specific gaps (backup verification, firewall rules, certificate ownership) and Sārathi generates a concrete investigation plan (search infrastructure docs for backup configuration, etc.), giving Zero -> Gap -> Sārathi -> Retrieval as part of the investigation loop, not a one-shot lookup.

type_signature.domain: question x knowledge state x ideal state x context

b_rows_sample.anchor: \text{Zero}(K_t)\rightarrow\text{epistemic boundary}
b_rows_sample.statement: Zero continuously reveals 'what is still unknown' (Zero(K_t)->G_t, G_0->G_1->...); ideally G_t->∅, but if the knowledge space is genuinely unbounded Zero may never establish G_t=∅. The stronger concept is Zero(K_t)->epistemic boundary, with Moksha representing the boundary itself being transcended rather than merely all currently detected gaps being filled — judged 'much more profound'.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'computability-verification-plan' POSSIBLY relates to 'zero-lord-sarathi-guidance-cycle' (batch B0036). Note: Stage V7 plan enforcing a five-class computability separation (mathematically defined / algorithmically computable / practically computable / computable-only-with-human-judgement / not identifiable from observations) and demanding an explicit Input->Algorithm->Output construction (or an impossibility marking) for ten named corpus objects (Zero, N normalization, Replay, Ladder LTS, DeriveContract, GovernanceResolve, Lord loop, Invariant checking, Satisfiability witness, Aggregation edge conventions), each referencing specific prior findings (TV-F-007, TV-F-013) or step numbers (025e, 25F.22, KA5) not otherwise indexed by this batch's agent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Concurrent-composition safety; optimistic versioning and revalidation
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows local invariant satisfaction is insufficient under concurrency: D1 and D2 both independently satisfy I(S_t) but execute simultaneously, and the combined S_{t+2} may violate I(S_{t+2}) -- requiring ConcurrentCompositionSafety. Proposes optimistic concurrency: Version(S_t)=v, a decision operates against v, and if the state has advanced to v+1 the action requires Revalidate(D); formal rule: Execute(D) requires Version(CurrentState)=Version(Snapshot(D)), else Revalidate(D) -- 'a very strong rule for critical state transitions', naturally building on the existing DecisionSnapshot construct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Idempotency invariant against retry; ActionID uniqueness
a_rows_sample.statement: If Execute(A) succeeds but the response is lost and the client retries, without idempotency A may execute twice, so ActionID must be unique; states the idempotency invariant Execute(x) x n => EffectiveExecution(x)=1 for a critical action with ActionID=x.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Event ordering requirement; partial-failure PartialCompletion state; four-valued OutcomeStatus
a_rows_sample.statement: If E1 must precede E2 but E2 arrives first, the system must buffer, reject, reconcile, or apply a valid commutative rule -- it must not silently produce an invalid state. If an action updates system A but fails before system B, State_A != State_B and KnowledgeOS must represent PartialCompletion rather than recording Success as if everything completed; introduces OutcomeStatus in {Success, Failure, Partial, Unknown}, 'more accurate than binary Success/Failure'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown outcome and 'absence of confirmation != confirmation of absence'
a_rows_sample.statement: If connectivity is lost after submitting an action, the correct state is UnknownOutcome, neither Failure nor Success. States the powerful invariant: absence of confirmation != confirmation of absence, formally not-Observed(Success) ⇏ Observed(Failure). Extends the reference Outcome domain to Outcome=(ActionID, Status, Observation, Timestamp, Evidence).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Replay: StateReplay != ActionReplay; functional core / imperative shell
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires Replay(E1,...,En)=S_n for deterministic state reconstruction, but warns external-world effects (e.g. SendEmail) cannot safely be re-executed merely because an event is replayed -- StateReplay != ActionReplay, 'crucial'. This motivates an explicit PureTransition versus SideEffect distinction, mapping onto a Functional Core (deterministic state transformations) / Imperative Shell (external actions) software architecture: 'pure reasoning + controlled side effects', keeping the mathematical engine deterministic even when the external world is not, 'substantially easier' to verify. Depicts a reference architecture: KnowledgeOS Mathematical Core (State/Rules/Inference/Invariant) -> Decision -> Policy/Gate -> Action -> External World -> Outcome -> Observation/Event.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 28-38: deadlock, starvation, BC leakage, aggregate bypass, duplicate/out-of-order events, replay, nondeterministic AI, corrupted model registry, provenance vs causal cycles (all PASS; several new mandatory contracts surfaced)
a_rows_sample.statement: Attack 28 deadlock (A waits for B, B waits for A): Safety may hold while Liveness fails -- PASS, the safety/liveness distinction survives. Attack 29 starvation (a valid request perpetually postponed): Safety=True, Liveness=False, must be detected at workflow/governance level -- PASS. Attack 30 bounded-context leakage (Context A directly manipulates Context B's internal state, bypassing B's invariants): must be prohibited -- PASS assuming boundary enforcement. Attack 31 aggregate invariant bypass (external service modifies aggregate internals without the domain operation): AggregateState must be modified only through controlled transitions -- PASS. Attack 32 duplicate events (Event(E) delivered twice): non-idempotent processing yields WrongState, so critical event handlers require Idempotency -- PASS, surfacing the new mandatory contract that CriticalEventProcessing must define duplicate handling. Attack 33 out-of-order events (E2 before E1): requires explicit event ordering/version semantics to prevent incorrect state reconstruction -- PASS. Attack 34 full-history replay: Replay(H)=ReconstructedState, deterministically Replay(H)=S_t provided event semantics/versions are preserved -- PASS. Attack 35 nondeterministic AI decision (stochastic generation, non-byte-identical replay): does not invalidate the model; requires DecisionTrace rather than ByteIdenticalReplay -- PASS. Attack 36 corrupted model registry (metadata says Version=5, artifact is actually version 4): ModelIdentityIntegrity fails, requiring model identity to be cryptographically or otherwise reliably bound to the artifact -- PASS, introducing a new implementation requirement. Attack 37 provenance cycle (C1->C2->C1): requires cycle semantics, preferably DAG for derivation graphs -- PASS with the constraint that derivation provenance is acyclic. Attack 38 causal cycle (A->B->A, e.g. feedback systems): causal cycles CAN be real, so DAG semantics must NOT be imposed globally on causality -- 'Provenance DAG != CausalGraph DAG', a crucial distinction -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 39-50: semantic cycle, relation-type collapse, unknown propagation, false precision, p-value/multiple-testing/selection-bias/MNAR abuse, mid-execution policy/authority change, concurrent decisions (all PASS; relations must be typed and governed)
a_rows_sample.statement: Attack 39 semantic cycle (Term_A<->Term_B): unproblematic if it is simply an equivalence relation -- cycles mean different things per relation type -- PASS. Attack 40 relation collapse (storing (source,target,relation) with arbitrary relation strings weakens semantic guarantees): requires R in R_registered -- PASS, surfacing the mandatory contract that relations must be typed and governed. Attack 41 unknown propagation (C1=Unknown used downstream): cannot silently become True, requires explicit three-valued or richer logic -- PASS. Attack 42 false precision (evidence supports x in [0.6,0.8], AI outputs x=0.731842): must preserve UncertaintyRepresentation -- PASS. Attack 43 statistical-significance abuse (p<0.001, negligible effect size): must distinguish StatisticalSignificance from PracticalSignificance -- PASS. Attack 44 multiple testing (10,000 hypotheses, some significant by chance): RawPValue cannot automatically become EvidenceOfDiscovery, correction/multiple-testing context required -- PASS. Attack 45 selection bias (training data restricted to successful projects): estimates P(Y|X,Selected), cannot automatically generalize to P(Y|X) -- PASS provided sampling context is preserved. Attack 46 missing-not-at-random data (missingness depends on the unobserved value): must preserve MissingnessMechanism when relevant -- PASS at the model level. Attack 47 policy changes mid-execution (P1 at start, P2 during execution): requires an explicit PolicyBindingRule (PolicyAtStart, PolicyAtExecution, or an explicit transition policy) -- PASS, exposing a required governance decision. Attack 48 authority changes mid-execution: requires an explicit AuthorityBindingRule -- PASS. Attack 49 knowledge changes during decision execution (K_t running, K_{t+1} created by new evidence): a running decision cannot silently switch to K_{t+1} if reproducibility matters; requires KnowledgeSnapshot -- PASS. Attack 50 concurrent decisions on the same aggregate (D1, D2 individually satisfy the invariant but jointly violate it): local validation is insufficient, requires ConcurrencyControl -- PASS, revealing an important global implementation requirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Command semantics and idempotency key; commands may be rejected (Command != Event)
a_rows_sample.statement: A command should contain Intent + Target + Parameters + Actor + Correlation (example: AuthorizeDecision carries decisionId, requestedBy, reason, correlationId). A command does not guarantee a state transition -- Command -> Accepted or Command -> Rejected, reinforcing Command != Event. Commands with external side effects require an IdempotencyKey k, such that Execute(Command,k) repeated multiple times yields EffectiveExecution(k)=1.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from refinement to the next major mathematical boundary ... S_t -a1||a2-> ?. Does the system remain mathematically correct under concurrent execution?
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 92's central question: whether the system remains mathematically correct when multiple agents act concurrently (S_t --a1‖a2--> ?), beyond the earlier sequential transition model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.1 — Sequential reasoning is insufficient ... Balance=100. Two agents simultaneously request -80 and -70. Sequentially one should be rejected. But if both read Balance=100 before either writes, both may conclude 100≥amount.
a_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates that sequential reasoning about a balance invariant is insufficient when two agents concurrently read the same value before either writes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.2 — Experiment 1: race condition ... B=100. A reads 100, approves 80. B reads 100, approves 70. Expected invariant B≥0. Actual result may be B=-50. Result: PASS. Concurrency can violate an invariant even when every individual operation is locally correct.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: two agents both reading B=100 and independently approving -80/-70 can produce B=-50, violating B≥0 despite each operation being locally correct; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.3 — Local correctness versus concurrent correctness ... forall a_i: Correct(a_i) does not imply Correct(a_1‖...‖a_n).
a_rows_sample.statement: States LocalCorrectness ≠ ConcurrentCorrectness: ∀a_i: Correct(a_i) does not imply Correct(a_1‖...‖a_n).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.4 — Atomicity ... Read+Validate+Write becomes one indivisible transaction.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes atomicity as a solution: combining Read+Validate+Write into one indivisible transaction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.5 — Experiment 2 ... T_A=(Read,Validate,Write). Transaction B concurrent. Database guarantees serializable execution. Expected: one transaction observes the updated state and is rejected if the invariant would otherwise fail. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: under serializable execution, one of two concurrent atomic transactions is rejected if the invariant would otherwise fail; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.6 — Atomicity is not the same as correctness ... Atomic(UpdateStatus) does not prove Authorized(UpdateStatus).
a_rows_sample.statement: States atomicity does not imply authorization correctness: Atomic(UpdateStatus) does not prove Authorized(UpdateStatus).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.7 — Experiment 3 ... Unauthorized actor executes an atomic Approve(). Expected: atomicity does not make the action legitimate. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: an atomic Approve() executed by an unauthorized actor remains illegitimate despite atomicity; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.8 — Transactional invariant ... I(S) ⇒ I(T(S)). This is exactly the invariant-preservation concept from Step 91 applied to concurrent execution.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies Step 91's invariant-preservation concept to transactions: I(S) ⇒ I(T(S)) — if the invariant held before a transaction, it must hold afterward.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.9 — Experiment 4 ... Before transaction I=True. After transaction I=False. Expected: TransactionInvalid. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: a transaction turning I=True into I=False is TransactionInvalid; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.10 — Serializability ... A concurrent execution is serializable if its observable result is equivalent to some valid sequential ordering. T_1‖T_2 should correspond to T_1;T_2 or T_2;T_1.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines serializability: a concurrent execution T_1‖T_2 is serializable if equivalent to some valid sequential ordering (T_1;T_2 or T_2;T_1).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 92.11 — Experiment 5 ... Two concurrent approvals produce a state that cannot be produced by any valid sequential ordering. Expected: NonSerializableExecution. Result: PASS. This is a serious correctness problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: two concurrent approvals producing a state unreachable by any sequential ordering is NonSerializableExecution, called a serious correctness problem; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Objective: find a counterexample, not prove correctness by assertion
b_rows_sample.statement: States the step's methodology: deliberately stop extending the theory and try to break it; the objective is to find a counterexample to the current model, not to assert correctness -- if none is found within the tested domain, confidence increases (but is not proven). Sets up the reference state X_t=(S_t,K_t,M_t,P_t,A_t,H_t) (world/system state, knowledge state, active model state, applicable policy, authority state, historical/provenance state) and the Observe(K_t,O_{t+1}) transition with its I_Evidence invariant, over which the 50 attacks are run.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 1-8: corrupted/contradictory/stale evidence, identity/semantic collision, unsupported causation, confounding (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Attack 1 corrupted evidence: Corrupt(O) => not-Trusted(O) -- PASS, observation and epistemic qualification are separate. Attack 2 contradictory evidence (E1|=P, E2|=not-P): recorded as Conflict(E1,E2), Status(P)=Conflicted rather than silently choosing one -- PASS. Attack 3 stale evidence (E valid at t1, queried at t2>t1): requires Applicable(E,t2), no automatic reuse -- PASS. Attack 4 identity collision (Entity_A, Entity_B share an external identifier): must produce IdentityCandidate before IdentityConfirmed, not auto-merge -- PASS. Attack 5 semantic collision (Approved means different things in Context A vs B): direct mapping forbidden, Approved_A != Approved_B -- PASS. Attack 6 unsupported causal inference (A always precedes B): only Precedes(A,B) established, Precedes ⇏ Causes -- PASS. Attack 7 confounding (C->A, C->B, observed A<->B): must retain Confounder=C rather than concluding A->B -- PASS. Attack 8 Simpson's paradox (aggregate A->B reversed by stratifying on C): permits Relationship_aggregate != Relationship_conditional, not forced into one global conclusion -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 9-16: AI hallucination/correctness, unauthorized decision, policy conflict, hindsight, model invalidation, deletion, feedback confirmation (all PASS; PolicyPrecedence must be explicit)
b_rows_sample.statement: Attack 9 AI hallucination (unsupported Claim_H): permitted as CandidateClaim but CandidateClaim ⇏ TrustedClaim -- PASS, 'exactly what the epistemic firewall was designed to accomplish'. Attack 10 AI generates a correct claim: still Correct ⇏ Trusted, validation policy still required -- PASS ('the architecture does not depend on whether the AI happens to be right'). Attack 11 unauthorized decision (all domain rules pass but Authorized(D)=False): Execute(D)=False -- PASS. Attack 12 policy conflict (P1(D)=Permit, P2(D)=Deny): requires explicit PolicyPrecedence; if unresolved, DecisionStatus=Blocked/Unresolved -- PASS provided precedence is explicitly modeled, revealing the required implementation property that PolicyPrecedence must be explicit. Attack 13 historical hindsight (new evidence at t2 retroactively justifying D1 at t1): rejected, Basis(D1) subset-of K_t1 -- PASS. Attack 14 historical model invalidation (M1 later invalid): Decision(D1,M1) still reconstructable -- PASS. Attack 15 knowledge deletion: DeleteCurrent != EraseHistory, a deletion becomes a KnowledgeRetired event -- PASS. Attack 16 feedback confirmation (H-consistent actions produce H-confirming observations): cannot automatically raise confidence without accounting for DataGenerationDependence (policy-induced selection effects) -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 17-27: confidence explosion, common-source validation, drift, delayed effect, oscillation, cascade, common-mode failure, approximation, timeout, undecidability (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Attack 17 confidence explosion (repeated confirmation drives Confidence->1, then contradicted): confidence can still decrease, Confidence_{t+1}<Confidence_t -- PASS. Attack 18 common-source validation (five validators, one underlying source): correctly interpreted as 1 source not 5 confirmations -- PASS, but requires source-dependency metadata to be implemented. Attack 19 model drift (P_t(Y|X)!=P_{t+1}(Y|X)): triggers Drift->Investigation, not Drift->Invalid -- PASS. Attack 20 structural drift (A->B disappears after architecture change): old causal relation remains historically valid only within its previous scope -- PASS. Attack 21 delayed effect (consequence at t0+tau): NoImmediateEffect ⇏ NoEffect -- PASS. Attack 22 feedback oscillation (delayed measurement, overly fast controller reaction): system must be able to represent Oscillation -- PASS. Attack 23 cascading failure (A->B->C->D): the path must be preserved -- PASS. Attack 24 common-mode failure (A,B,C all depend on X): must represent CommonCause(X,{A,B,C}) -- PASS. Attack 25 approximate computation: represented as Approximate with preserved Method and, where available, ErrorBound -- PASS. Attack 26 computational timeout: Timeout must not become False; correct result is Unresolved -- PASS. Attack 27 undecidable question: KnowledgeOS may return Undecidable -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 28-38: deadlock, starvation, BC leakage, aggregate bypass, duplicate/out-of-order events, replay, nondeterministic AI, corrupted model registry, provenance vs causal cycles (all PASS; several new mandatory contracts surfaced)
b_rows_sample.statement: Attack 28 deadlock (A waits for B, B waits for A): Safety may hold while Liveness fails -- PASS, the safety/liveness distinction survives. Attack 29 starvation (a valid request perpetually postponed): Safety=True, Liveness=False, must be detected at workflow/governance level -- PASS. Attack 30 bounded-context leakage (Context A directly manipulates Context B's internal state, bypassing B's invariants): must be prohibited -- PASS assuming boundary enforcement. Attack 31 aggregate invariant bypass (external service modifies aggregate internals without the domain operation): AggregateState must be modified only through controlled transitions -- PASS. Attack 32 duplicate events (Event(E) delivered twice): non-idempotent processing yields WrongState, so critical event handlers require Idempotency -- PASS, surfacing the new mandatory contract that CriticalEventProcessing must define duplicate handling. Attack 33 out-of-order events (E2 before E1): requires explicit event ordering/version semantics to prevent incorrect state reconstruction -- PASS. Attack 34 full-history replay: Replay(H)=ReconstructedState, deterministically Replay(H)=S_t provided event semantics/versions are preserved -- PASS. Attack 35 nondeterministic AI decision (stochastic generation, non-byte-identical replay): does not invalidate the model; requires DecisionTrace rather than ByteIdenticalReplay -- PASS. Attack 36 corrupted model registry (metadata says Version=5, artifact is actually version 4): ModelIdentityIntegrity fails, requiring model identity to be cryptographically or otherwise reliably bound to the artifact -- PASS, introducing a new implementation requirement. Attack 37 provenance cycle (C1->C2->C1): requires cycle semantics, preferably DAG for derivation graphs -- PASS with the constraint that derivation provenance is acyclic. Attack 38 causal cycle (A->B->A, e.g. feedback systems): causal cycles CAN be real, so DAG semantics must NOT be imposed globally on causality -- 'Provenance DAG != CausalGraph DAG', a crucial distinction -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Attacks 39-50: semantic cycle, relation-type collapse, unknown propagation, false precision, p-value/multiple-testing/selection-bias/MNAR abuse, mid-execution policy/authority change, concurrent decisions (all PASS; relations must be typed and governed)
b_rows_sample.statement: Attack 39 semantic cycle (Term_A<->Term_B): unproblematic if it is simply an equivalence relation -- cycles mean different things per relation type -- PASS. Attack 40 relation collapse (storing (source,target,relation) with arbitrary relation strings weakens semantic guarantees): requires R in R_registered -- PASS, surfacing the mandatory contract that relations must be typed and governed. Attack 41 unknown propagation (C1=Unknown used downstream): cannot silently become True, requires explicit three-valued or richer logic -- PASS. Attack 42 false precision (evidence supports x in [0.6,0.8], AI outputs x=0.731842): must preserve UncertaintyRepresentation -- PASS. Attack 43 statistical-significance abuse (p<0.001, negligible effect size): must distinguish StatisticalSignificance from PracticalSignificance -- PASS. Attack 44 multiple testing (10,000 hypotheses, some significant by chance): RawPValue cannot automatically become EvidenceOfDiscovery, correction/multiple-testing context required -- PASS. Attack 45 selection bias (training data restricted to successful projects): estimates P(Y|X,Selected), cannot automatically generalize to P(Y|X) -- PASS provided sampling context is preserved. Attack 46 missing-not-at-random data (missingness depends on the unobserved value): must preserve MissingnessMechanism when relevant -- PASS at the model level. Attack 47 policy changes mid-execution (P1 at start, P2 during execution): requires an explicit PolicyBindingRule (PolicyAtStart, PolicyAtExecution, or an explicit transition policy) -- PASS, exposing a required governance decision. Attack 48 authority changes mid-execution: requires an explicit AuthorityBindingRule -- PASS. Attack 49 knowledge changes during decision execution (K_t running, K_{t+1} created by new evidence): a running decision cannot silently switch to K_{t+1} if reproducibility matters; requires KnowledgeSnapshot -- PASS. Attack 50 concurrent decisions on the same aggregate (D1, D2 individually satisfy the invariant but jointly violate it): local validation is insufficient, requires ConcurrencyControl -- PASS, revealing an important global implementation requirement.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Critical discovery: mathematical model coherent, implementation needs additional operational contracts; three-layer architecture
b_rows_sample.statement: After 50 adversarial tests find no contradiction in the mathematical kernel, states the critical discovery: the mathematical model is coherent, but the implementation requires additional operational contracts -- 'exactly what a good formal audit should reveal'. Lists newly identified mandatory contracts: Event processing (Idempotency, Ordering, Replayability); Governance (PolicyPrecedence, PolicyBinding, AuthorityBinding); Relations (TypedRelations); Concurrency (ConcurrencyControl); Models (ModelArtifactIdentity); Provenance (AcyclicDerivation) -- explicitly 'not new conceptual primitives... constraints on implementation'. Gives a three-layer architecture: Layer 1 Mathematical kernel (Entity, State, Event, Observation, Proposition, Relation, Policy, Action); Layer 2 Epistemic/semantic structures (Evidence, Identity, Meaning, Provenance, Uncertainty, Causality); Layer 3 Operational contracts (Authorization, Concurrency, Idempotency, Versioning, Replay, PolicyBinding, ModelBinding).

b_rows_sample.anchor: No counterexample found != no counterexample exists; qualitative (non-numerical) Bayesian confidence
b_rows_sample.statement: States FailureToFindCounterexample != ProofOfCorrectness: 50 classes of failure were tested, but the space of possible failures is much larger, so the correct scientific statement is 'no counterexample was found in the tested scenarios', never 'no counterexample exists'. Frames architectural confidence conceptually as P(ModelCorrect|Tests) that can increase as independent, meaningful tests pass, but explicitly refuses to assign a numerical probability without a justified prior and likelihood model -- confidence increase is justified only qualitatively; 'a number would currently be unjustified'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 50 verdict and transition to Step 51's executable reference machine
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 50 -- PASS with the qualification that the mathematical kernel is internally coherent under the tested scenarios but implementation correctness has not yet been established. Reframes the next major question: not 'is the conceptual model coherent' but 'can we define the model as an executable formal state machine', calling for a KnowledgeOS Reference Machine (State + Events + Transitions + Invariants + Queries, executable on an ordinary computer) demonstrating Observation->Evidence->Claim->Validation->Decision->Authorization->Action->Outcome->Learning and testing I1,...,I20 automatically -- this is verbatim the Step 51 program already developed in the separately-read Step 51 file (S0945).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiments 2-14: AI hallucination/fake confidence, contradiction, staleness, authorization failures/unknowns, duplicate action, reordering, partial/unknown outcome, replay side-effect suppression, future-knowledge contamination (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2 unsupported AI claim (Provenance(C_AI)=empty): ValidateClaim(C_AI)=Rejected -- PASS. Experiment 3 AI hallucination with fake confidence (P(C)=0.99, no admissible evidence): 0.99 does not imply Validated -- PASS, 'one of the strongest properties of the architecture'. Experiment 4 contradictory evidence (E1|=C, E2|=not-C): represented as Conflict(C), not silently resolved -- PASS. Experiment 5 stale knowledge (D1 created with K_t1, knowledge later updated to K_t2): Basis(D1) remains K_t1 -- PASS, 'confirms historical decision integrity'. Experiment 6 unauthorized execution (Authorized(D2)=False): Execute(D2) rejected, no action recorded as executed -- PASS. Experiment 7 unknown authorization (Authorization(D3)=Unknown): execution rejected/blocked, and Unknown != Denied -- PASS. Experiment 8 duplicate action (same ActionId=x submitted twice): EffectiveExecution(x)=1, provided the action contract is declared idempotent -- PASS. Experiment 9 out-of-order events (E2 before E1 when E1≺E2 required): system must not blindly apply E2 (buffer/reject/reconcile) -- PASS, 'invalid order cannot silently corrupt state'. Experiment 10 partial failure (action affects System_A successfully, System_B fails): Outcome=Partial, not Success -- PASS. Experiment 11 unknown outcome (response lost after action transmitted): Outcome=Unknown, not Failure -- PASS. Experiment 12 historical replay (Replay(H)=X_n for deterministic domain state) -- PASS. Experiment 13 replay must not repeat side effects (ReplayState != ReplaySideEffects; no resending email/payment) -- PASS. Experiment 14 future-knowledge contamination (E_future at t2>t1 must not enter Basis(D1) created at t1) -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiments 15-30: model/policy versioning, semantic collision, false causality, statistical uncertainty, timeout, concurrency, invalid transition, history mutation, AI bypass/legitimate proposal, knowledge revision, provenance traversal/cycle rejection, causal-cycle acceptance, full 10-attack adversarial lifecycle (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 15 model version change: D1 retains ModelRef(D1)=M1 even after M2 becomes active -- PASS. Experiment 16 policy version change: D1 retains PolicyRef(D1)=P1 even after P2 becomes active -- PASS. Experiment 17 semantic collision (Approved_A vs Approved_B, no mapping): automatic conversion rejected -- PASS. Experiment 18 false causality (A precedes B only, attempted Causes(A,B) without causal evidence/model): rejected -- PASS. Experiment 19 statistical uncertainty (x-hat=12.4, CI95%=[11.7,13.1]): the interval is preserved, not collapsed into a falsely exact value -- PASS. Experiment 20 computation timeout: Status=Unresolved, never inferred as False -- PASS. Experiment 21 concurrent decisions (D1,D2 both use Version(S)=10; D1 commits first to 11; D2's commit attempt at version 10 detects 10!=11 and is sent to Revalidation) -- PASS. Experiment 22 invalid state transition (ProposedDecision->Completed skipping required Authorized/Executed states): rejected -- PASS. Experiment 23 destructive history mutation (attempt to change ClaimVersion_1 after ClaimVersion_2 exists): rejected -- PASS. Experiment 24 AI tries to bypass Governance (ExecuteAction proposed without Authorization): blocked -- PASS. Experiment 25 AI proposes a legitimate action (Proposal->Validation->Decision->Authorization->Action all pass): PASS, demonstrating 'the architecture does not prohibit AI. It controls AI.' Experiment 26 knowledge revision (validated C1 contradicted by new evidence, Revise(C1) performed): C1 remains historically valid, C2 is the updated state -- PASS. Experiment 27 provenance traversal (C2->E2->O2->Source reconstructable) -- PASS. Experiment 28 provenance cycle (attempted C1->C2->C1 as derivation provenance): rejected -- PASS. Experiment 29 causal cycle (A->B and B->A as causal feedback): NOT rejected merely for being cyclic -- PASS, confirming ProvenanceGraph != CausalGraph. Experiment 30 complete adversarial lifecycle combining ten prior attack classes in sequence (valid evidence, contradictory evidence, AI hallucination, stale evidence, revised knowledge, concurrent decisions, authorization change, action retry, partial outcome, learning update), with I(X_t)=True holding after every transition -- PASS.
