a_rows_sample.anchor: S_A -signal-> M_A -perception-> O_B -interpretation-> H_B -assessment-> K_B -response-> R_B. Then the response becomes new evidence for A: R_B -> O_A -> K_A'. So we have A -> B -> A -> B -> ... This is a distributed epistemic feedback loop.
a_rows_sample.statement: Models multi-round animal courtship as a distributed epistemic feedback loop richer than a one-shot alarm-call model: S_A-signal->M_A-perception->O_B-interpretation->H_B-assessment->K_B-response->R_B, with the response becoming new evidence feeding back into A (R_B->O_A->K_A'), giving the cyclic pattern A->B->A->B->...

b_rows_sample.anchor: (S,I,M,R,A,O) where S=signaller, I=internal/private state, M=message/signal, R=receiver interpretation, A=action, O=outcome. ... I_S -Encode-> M -Interpret_R-> K_R -Decision-> A. That is potentially a communication algebra.
b_rows_sample.statement: Abstracts animal signalling-game theory (a signaller with private information, a signal, a receiver, receiver interpretation, receiver decision, and consequences for both parties) into a candidate 6-tuple (S,I,M,R,A,O) and a processing chain I_S-Encode->M-Interpret_R->K_R-Decision->A, proposed as the seed of a candidate 'communication algebra' for KnowledgeOS.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'courtship-reciprocal-feedback-loop' POSSIBLY relates to 'signalling-game-formalization' (batch B0067). Note: A multi-round reciprocal courtship communication loop, extending the single-round signalling-game formalization from S2818.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Critical thinking can be used as an epistemic interrogation process that reconstructs the current state of knowledge from a body of claims, evidence, assumptions, inferences, concepts, perspectives, and implications. The important distinction is that the book does not provide a quantitative "knowledge state" formula. But it gives us a remarkably useful state-extraction framework.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reformulates the user's hypothesis into: critical thinking can be used as an epistemic interrogation process that reconstructs the current state of knowledge from a body of claims, evidence, assumptions, inferences, concepts, perspectives, and implications; notes Paul & Elder's book itself provides a qualitative state-extraction framework, not a quantitative knowledge-state formula.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Paul & Elder explicitly decompose reasoning into eight Elements of Thought: Purpose, Question at issue, Information, Interpretation/inference, Concepts, Assumptions, Point of view, Implications/consequences. ... Document -> Critical interrogation -> Epistemic structure [Questions, Claims/inferences, Information/evidence, Concepts, Assumptions, Perspectives, Implications, Purpose]
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Paul & Elder's eight Elements of Thought (Purpose, Question at issue, Information, Interpretation/inference, Concepts, Assumptions, Point of view, Implications/consequences) as the raw state dimensions for an extraction pipeline replacing simple Document->summary with Document->Critical interrogation->Epistemic structure (Questions/Claims-inferences/Information-evidence/Concepts/Assumptions/Perspectives/Implications/Purpose).

a_rows_sample.anchor: the book proposes standards such as: Clarity, Accuracy, Precision, Relevance, Depth, Breadth, Logic, Significance, Fairness and explicitly says these standards should be applied to the elements of reasoning. So we can construct a matrix ... This is much more informative than one knowledge score.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Paul & Elder's nine Intellectual Standards (Clarity, Accuracy, Precision, Relevance, Depth, Breadth, Logic, Significance, Fairness), applied to reasoning elements, illustrated as a Knowledge-element x Standard matrix (e.g. Claim A/Claim B/Assumption C scored against all nine columns), argued to be much more informative than a single knowledge score.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would not define: Knowledge = Score. Instead: KnowledgeState(t) = {Claims,Evidence,Relations,Assumptions,Uncertainty,Perspectives,Validity}_t. Then critical thinking evaluates the state. For a claim (c): KS(c,t) = [Evidence, Inference, Assumptions, Perspective, Contradictions, Clarity, Accuracy, Precision, Relevance, Depth, Breadth, Logic, Significance, Fairness]. This becomes an epistemic state vector.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects Knowledge=Score, defining instead KnowledgeState(t)={Claims,Evidence,Relations,Assumptions,Uncertainty,Perspectives,Validity}_t as the corpus-level state that critical thinking evaluates, and a per-claim 14-component epistemic state vector KS(c,t)=[Evidence, Inference, Assumptions, Perspective, Contradictions, Clarity, Accuracy, Precision, Relevance, Depth, Breadth, Logic, Significance, Fairness].
a_rows_sample.type_signature: KnowledgeState(t) = {Claims,Evidence,Relations,Assumptions,Uncertainty,Perspectives,Validity}_t; KS(c,t) = [Evidence, Inference, Assumptions, Perspective, Contradictions, Clarity, Accuracy, Precision, Relevance, Depth, Breadth, Logic, Significance, Fairness]

a_rows_sample.anchor: This fits your previous insight perfectly. ... Critical thinking does not simply delete C1. It performs a state transition: CURRENT -> RE-EVALUATION -> C1 remains historically valid / C1 loses current validity / C2 becomes current. Therefore: K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_new).
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the batch's temporal-knowledge-trajectory model into the critical-thinking framework: when new evidence appears (e.g. C1='Architecture A is used' superseded by C2='Architecture A was replaced by B'), critical thinking performs a state transition rather than deletion -- C1 remains historically valid but loses current validity while C2 becomes current -- formalized as K_{t+1}=Update(K_t, E_new).

a_rows_sample.anchor: the book explicitly distinguishes information from inference and assumptions. So we can classify: OBSERVATION -> INFORMATION -> CLAIM -> INFERENCE -> JUSTIFICATION while separately tracking: ASSUMPTION, OPINION, PERSPECTIVE, PREFERENCE, IMPLICATION, UNCERTAINTY. This is exactly where your earlier inverse statistical approach becomes interesting. Instead of asking "What knowledge does this document contain?" we ask: "What can survive systematic attempts to disprove, weaken, contextualize, or reinterpret its claims?"
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses Paul & Elder's information/inference/assumption distinction to separate a core knowledge-candidate pipeline (OBSERVATION->INFORMATION->CLAIM->INFERENCE->JUSTIFICATION) from a separately-tracked non-knowledge-adjacent set (ASSUMPTION, OPINION, PERSPECTIVE, PREFERENCE, IMPLICATION, UNCERTAINTY); explicitly connects this to the batch's earlier inverse-statistical/not-knowledge approach by reframing the extraction question from 'what knowledge does this document contain?' to 'what can survive systematic attempts to disprove, weaken, contextualize, or reinterpret its claims?'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The book says reasoning should actively search for information that opposes a position, not merely information supporting it. ... CLAIM -> supporting evidence? / contradictory evidence? / hidden assumptions? / alternative interpretation? / alternative viewpoint? / implications? / contradictions? -> RE-EVALUATED CLAIM. This is much closer to knowledge discovery than conventional NLP summarization.
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames critical thinking as an adversarial knowledge filter: reasoning must actively search for opposing (not merely supporting) evidence, systematically interrogating each claim for supporting/contradictory evidence, hidden assumptions, alternative interpretations/viewpoints, implications, and contradictions before producing a re-evaluated claim; characterized as much closer to knowledge discovery than conventional NLP summarization.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Now we have three powerful operations. Dhatu / linguistic lens: What is the structural meaning expressed by the language? Critical-thinking lens: What claims, evidence, assumptions and inferences are actually justified? Zero lens: What remains after removing language, rhetoric, terminology and representation? So: Text -> SemanticStructure -> EpistemicStructure -> InvariantStructure. That is starting to look like an actual Knowledge Extraction Engine.
a_rows_sample.statement: Combines three research lenses into a single pipeline: the Dhatu/linguistic lens (structural meaning expressed by language), the critical-thinking lens (which claims/evidence/assumptions/inferences are actually justified), and the Zero lens (what remains after removing language/rhetoric/terminology/representation), yielding Text -> SemanticStructure -> EpistemicStructure -> InvariantStructure, described as an actual 'Knowledge Extraction Engine'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: State(K,t) = [N_c number of claims, N_e evidence coverage, N_a assumption load, N_x contradictions, N_u uncertainty, C coherence, R relevance, B breadth, D depth, I invariance]. Then we can study: Delta State = State(K,t2)-State(K,t1). Now we can actually say: The knowledge state became more complete, but less certain. ... That is far more meaningful than: "Knowledge increased from 73 to 81."
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes quantifying the corpus STATE rather than 'knowledge' itself, via a ten-component vector State(K,t)=[claim count Nc, evidence coverage Ne, assumption load Na, contradictions Nx, uncertainty Nu, coherence C, relevance R, breadth B, depth D, invariance I], and a delta DeltaState=State(K,t2)-State(K,t1) that yields qualitative, multi-dimensional descriptions of change (e.g. 'more complete but less certain', 'gained evidence but accumulated contradictions', 'more precise but lost breadth') instead of an opaque scalar change like 'knowledge increased from 73 to 81'.
a_rows_sample.type_signature: State(K,t) = [N_c, N_e, N_a, N_x, N_u, C, R, B, D, I]; ΔState = State(K,t2) − State(K,t1)

a_rows_sample.anchor: It distinguishes questions requiring a single system and evidence/reasoning toward a correct answer, subjective questions where there is no assessable answer in the same sense, and multi-system questions where evidence and reasoning can produce better or worse judgments. That means our KnowledgeOS shouldn't treat every statement as the same epistemic object. We potentially need: QuestionType in {Definitive, Subjective, MultiPerspective}
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Paul & Elder's three-kinds-of-questions distinction (Definitive: single system, evidence/reasoning toward a correct answer; Subjective: no assessable answer in the same sense; MultiPerspective/multi-system: evidence and reasoning can produce better or worse judgments), concluding KnowledgeOS must not treat every statement as the same kind of epistemic object, proposing QuestionType in {Definitive, Subjective, MultiPerspective} with evaluation model varying by type.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Critical reasoning can be used to reconstruct and evaluate the epistemic state of a knowledge corpus at a given point in time. ... KnowledgeState(t) = CriticalAnalysis(Claims,Evidence,Inferences,Assumptions,Concepts,Perspectives,Implications) ... Evaluation = UniversalIntellectualStandards ... KnowledgeState(t+1) = Update(KnowledgeState(t), NewEvidence, NewArguments, NewContradictions). That gives us a dynamic epistemic model, rather than a static knowledge database.
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the file's central research proposition -- critical reasoning can be used to reconstruct and evaluate the epistemic state of a knowledge corpus at a given point in time -- and consolidates it into three boxed formulas: KnowledgeState(t)=CriticalAnalysis(Claims,Evidence,Inferences,Assumptions,Concepts,Perspectives,Implications); Evaluation=UniversalIntellectualStandards; KnowledgeState(t+1)=Update(KnowledgeState(t), NewEvidence, NewArguments, NewContradictions); concludes this gives a dynamic epistemic model rather than a static knowledge database, and is a stronger research direction than inventing a single 'knowledge quantity'.
a_rows_sample.type_signature: KnowledgeState(t) = CriticalAnalysis(Claims,Evidence,Inferences,Assumptions,Concepts,Perspectives,Implications); Evaluation = UniversalIntellectualStandards; KnowledgeState(t+1) = Update(KnowledgeState(t), NewEvidence, NewArguments, NewContradictions)

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is a continuously changing body of facts, observations, and justified relationships about a changing reality. The important word is continuously. Knowledge is therefore not a static object like: Knowledge = {fact1, fact2, fact3, ...}
b_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens a user-proposed formulation into 'Knowledge is a continuously changing body of facts, observations, and justified relationships about a changing reality', emphasizing 'continuously' and rejecting the static-set model Knowledge={fact1,fact2,fact3,...}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A fact is not simply: "X is true." It is closer to: F = (claim, evidence, context, time, source, validity). So: Knowledge(t) is a state of accumulated and structured facts at time (t). Then: Knowledge(t1) != Knowledge(t2) because ... new facts appear, old facts are confirmed, old facts are contradicted, facts become obsolete, interpretations change, relationships between facts change, confidence changes.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a fact as a structured tuple F=(claim, evidence, context, time, source, validity) rather than a bare truth-claim, and Knowledge(t) as the state of accumulated/structured facts at time t, such that Knowledge(t1) != Knowledge(t2) in general because facts appear, are confirmed or contradicted, become obsolete, interpretations change, relationships change, and confidence changes.
b_rows_sample.type_signature: F = (claim, evidence, context, time, source, validity); Knowledge(t1) ≠ Knowledge(t2)

b_rows_sample.anchor: t1: "The system uses architecture A." Later t2: "The system migrated to architecture B." The old statement wasn't necessarily false knowledge at t1. It was: Valid(F,t1)=true but: Valid(F,t2)=false or perhaps: Status(F,t2)=historical. ... KnowledgeOS should probably not "delete" the old fact. It should preserve the trajectory ... knowledge has temporal semantics.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Knowledge from Truth via a system-architecture migration example: the old statement was not false knowledge at t1 (Valid(F,t1)=true) but becomes invalid or historical at t2 (Valid(F,t2)=false, or Status(F,t2)=historical); establishes the principle that KnowledgeOS should not delete superseded facts but preserve their validity trajectory, i.e. knowledge has temporal semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reality changes: R(t). Observations of reality change: O(t). Our justified representation of those observations changes: K(t). Therefore: K(t)=f(O_<=t,E_<=t,C_<=t) ... Knowledge is therefore a continuously evolving state, not a document.
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes the temporal model: reality R(t), observations O(t), and justified representation K(t) all change over time, giving K(t)=f(O_<=t, E_<=t, C_<=t) (a function of observations, evidence, and contextual interpretation up to time t); knowledge is a continuously evolving state, not a document.

b_rows_sample.anchor: REALITY -> OBSERVATIONS -> EVIDENCE -> FACT / CLAIM STATE -> RELATIONSHIPS -> KNOWLEDGE -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> {current, historical}. And every knowledge element has a lifecycle.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a revised KnowledgeOS architecture pipeline replacing the simple Documents->Knowledge model: REALITY -> OBSERVATIONS -> EVIDENCE -> FACT/CLAIM STATE -> RELATIONSHIPS -> KNOWLEDGE -> KNOWLEDGE STATE, branching into current vs historical; every knowledge element is asserted to have a lifecycle.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Davidson's invariance idea then becomes a way of distinguishing: What changes: representation, language, measurement, interpretation, model from: What remains invariant: relationships, truth conditions, structural properties. Davidson explicitly frames invariance as significant pattern and structure that remains under different forms of representation. So our model could become: Knowledge = Temporal Fact State + Relations + Evidence + Invariants.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends an existing Davidson-invariance idea into the temporal knowledge model: distinguishes what changes (representation, language, measurement, interpretation, model) from what remains invariant (relationships, truth conditions, structural properties), yielding the formalization Knowledge = Temporal Fact State + Relations + Evidence + Invariants.
b_rows_sample.type_signature: Knowledge = Temporal Fact State + Relations + Evidence + Invariants

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would not define knowledge simply as "facts." Because facts can exist without anybody knowing them. For example: A particular physical event happened yesterday, but nobody observed it. It is a fact. It is not necessarily knowledge for anyone. So I would distinguish: Fact != Knowledge. Instead: Knowledge = Facts/claims + Evidence + Justification + Context + Temporal validity + Relationships. And because all of these can change: Knowledge = K(t).
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects an implicit 'knowledge = facts' equation via a counterexample (an unobserved physical event is a fact but knowledge for nobody), establishing Fact != Knowledge, and redefines Knowledge = Facts/claims + Evidence + Justification + Context + Temporal validity + Relationships = K(t), since all of these components can change over time.
b_rows_sample.type_signature: Fact ≠ Knowledge; Knowledge = Facts/claims + Evidence + Justification + Context + Temporal validity + Relationships = K(t)

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not: "How much knowledge does a system contain?" but: "What is the current state of its continuously evolving body of justified facts, and how did that state change over time?" That naturally leads us toward knowledge as a temporal state machine / knowledge trajectory, rather than knowledge as a static repository.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the file's conceptual conclusion: reframe the guiding question from 'how much knowledge does a system contain?' to 'what is the current state of its continuously evolving body of justified facts, and how did that state change over time?', proposing knowledge as a temporal state machine/trajectory rather than a static repository -- offered as a candidate foundation for the KnowledgeOS model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This fits your previous insight perfectly. ... Critical thinking does not simply delete C1. It performs a state transition: CURRENT -> RE-EVALUATION -> C1 remains historically valid / C1 loses current validity / C2 becomes current. Therefore: K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_new).
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the batch's temporal-knowledge-trajectory model into the critical-thinking framework: when new evidence appears (e.g. C1='Architecture A is used' superseded by C2='Architecture A was replaced by B'), critical thinking performs a state transition rather than deletion -- C1 remains historically valid but loses current validity while C2 becomes current -- formalized as K_{t+1}=Update(K_t, E_new).
